rationale: The repair experiment executed (CheckRun 183f75213c5a4f26a951f76784b3e54f, 19 events). Its declared comparison did not resolve because the correlation expected the repair pair at other indices, but the pair is present and complete at indices 15 and 16: the restarted node's configuration is empty and becomes the full configuration in force after a later configuration entry arrives, which bounds the configuration gap. The same receipt also contains the authority-transition probe's events at indices 17 and 18, where a node that is no longer in the configuration forced a leadership change; that question is registered here with its own experiment and comparisons.

investigations.question: Can a server that is no longer part of the configuration trigger a leadership change by sending TimeoutNow to a voter, given that the TimeoutNow handler neither verifies the sender nor that a transfer is in progress, while vote requests carrying the leadership-transfer flag suppress the rejection for nodes that already know a leader?
investigations.hypothesis: timeoutNow sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer regardless of who sent the request, so a removed server's message makes the recipient campaign with the transfer flag set; voters then grant their votes although they have a healthy leader, because the leader-availability rejection is skipped when LeadershipTransfer is set, and the serving leader steps down when it observes the higher term.
investigations.discriminator: Remove one node from a three-voter configuration, have that removed node send TimeoutNow over the transport to a surviving follower, and observe the follower's state and term, the serving leader's state, and which node leads afterwards.

interpretations.rationale: Current account of the repair side of this question: the configuration gap closes as soon as any configuration entry reaches the node. Parsed event 15 records the restarted node with an empty live configuration while its log records the two voters of the configuration in force; parsed event 16 records that after the serving leader commits AddNonvoter at index 8 the node's live configuration becomes the three servers of the configuration in force (two voters plus the added nonvoter), and config_repaired_by_later_entry is true. So the window opened by the restart is bounded by the next configuration entry or installed snapshot, which is what the earlier account listed as counterevidence; the underlying defect is unchanged, since the node's configuration was empty from NewRaft until that entry arrived, and its own log already recorded the configuration in force. The declared comparison for this receipt could not be resolved because the correlation expected the setup/result pair at indices that do not carry it; the pair is present and complete at indices 15 and 16, which is what this account cites.
counterevidence: This receipt shows the repair path working, which limits the duration of the gap but not the reading that the node was wrong when it started: before the new entry arrived, the node had an empty configuration while its log recorded the configuration in force.
The repair in this receipt required an explicit configuration change; a cluster with no membership churn after the restart would leave the node in the wrong configuration indefinitely.
The comparison for this receipt was recorded as unresolved because of correlation indices, so this account cites the parsed events directly rather than the comparison outcome.
limitations: Measured on a two-peer in-memory cluster with commit-tracking stores and snapshotting disabled; the empty (rather than stale) case is the one exercised.

The repair entry was committed by the surviving leader while the restarted node was still a member of the configuration in force; a node that is itself removed by the missed entry would not receive such an entry in the same way.
Only the arriving-configuration-entry path was measured; the installed-snapshot repair path is source-derived.

scope.description: A three-voter in-memory cluster with a serving leader: one follower is removed with RemoveServer, the removed node is allowed to receive the entry that drops it from the configuration, and then that removed node sends a TimeoutNow request over the transport to the remaining follower while the leader is healthy. The probe records the configuration in force, the removed node's membership, the target's state and term before and after, the serving leader's state, and who leads afterwards.
assumptions: Cluster, transports and FSM are the repository's own MakeCluster, InmemTransport and MockFSM facilities, and the removal uses the public RemoveServer API.
The removed node stays transport-reachable, which is the situation for a server that has been taken out of the configuration but not shut down.
The request is delivered through the same transport method the library uses for leadership transfer.

experiment.prefix: Start a three-voter cluster, wait for a leader and commit one command; choose a follower to remove and another follower as target; RemoveServer the first one and wait until the removed node's own configuration no longer contains it; emit the setup event with the configuration in force, the removed node's membership, the target's state and term, and the leader; send TimeoutNow from the removed node's transport to the target, wait until the target is leader or leadership changes, then emit the result event with the timeout error, the target's state and term, the old leader's state and whether it stepped down, whether a leader is present afterwards and whether the target became it.
experiment.requirement: Only the current leader of the configuration in force may trigger a leadership transfer; a server outside that configuration must not be able to make a voter campaign or to displace the serving leader.
experiment.responsibility: Raft itself: the TimeoutNow handler decides what a received transfer trigger means, and the vote handler decides how much trust to extend to a transfer-flagged campaign.

comparisons.description: A server outside the configuration in force cannot change who leads.
The serving leader keeps its authority when a non-member sends a transfer trigger.
